Calamity

/kuh-LAM-uh-tee/ — rhymes with vanity · noun

Hear It

What It Means

A calamity is a sudden event that causes serious damage, loss, or suffering, like a natural disaster.

The dam burst was a calamity that emptied three villages overnight.

Worked Example

When the hurricane destroyed the coastal town's hospital, leaving thousands without shelter or medical care, it was a calamity unlike anything residents had ever witnessed.

The word calamity emphasizes the sudden, catastrophic nature and widespread human suffering of a major disaster. While 'disaster' is a synonym, calamity stresses the human toll and sudden rupture of normal life more deeply.

How Calamity Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

disaster

disaster: a sudden event causing great damage

tragedy

tragedy: a deeply sad event bringing suffering

mishap

mishap: a small unlucky accident, far milder

Antonyms

blessing

blessing: a welcome event that brings good

boon

boon: a timely benefit or great help

How Strong Is It? — setback → misfortune → disaster → calamity

setback vs. calamity

setback vs. calamity: A setback is far weaker than a calamity: a setback delays your progress, while a calamity brings sudden, serious damage and suffering.

misfortune vs. calamity

misfortune vs. calamity: Misfortune is weaker than calamity — misfortune is ordinary bad luck, but a calamity is a devastating event that causes real loss and grief.

disaster vs. calamity

disaster vs. calamity: Disaster is strong, yet calamity reaches even further on this scale: a disaster causes great damage, while a calamity emphasizes the deep, widespread suffering left behind.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — calam

Root — calam: damage, loss, disaster (from Latin calamitas)

Suffix — -ity

Suffix — -ity: state or quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Calam ('damage, loss, disaster,' from Latin calamitas) + -ity ('state of') — a calamity is a state of serious damage and loss brought on by a sudden, destructive event. (An old story ties it to calamus, 'straw,' as in ruined crops, but etymologists now call that folk etymology.)

Use the root in a new word: calamitous

Use the root in a new word: calamitous: The calamitous storm left the coastline in ruins — calamitous simply adds the adjective ending -ous to the same Latin root calamit-, 'disaster and loss,' that gives us calamity.

Word Building

Word Choice

formal / literary

Calamity stresses sudden, widespread suffering and loss. Reach for it when describing a major disaster—natural, political, or social—that affects many people. For smaller problems, use 'disaster' or 'mishap'.
